nodes.title: The overnight loop's human interface is a 114-item queue of 6,684 changed lines
nodes.body: The measured promotion queue is 6,684 changed lines across 114 patches (exp-human-007). Treat that as the interface's actual input: a supervisor waking at 06:00 faces 114 independent patch decisions, about 59 changed lines per decision. Two mechanisms follow. First, at any plausible dwell budget the human cannot inspect 114 items at line level, so the effective decision is triage, not review. Second, the loop's own scoring is binary (exp-score-001) and minGain never changed a decision (exp-gate-001), so the queue cannot be pre-sorted by quality margin: every item looks equally "passed". Falsifiable prediction: an interface that caps the morning queue at K items and defers the rest will lower defect escape rate per reviewed patch relative to a 114-item flat list at equal total review minutes, because triage effort is reallocated to items the human can actually inspect.

nodes.title: A green check from this verifier carries almost no information: 89 of 94 verifiers already pass on the clean base tree
nodes.body: Two ledger measurements combine into a hard claim about what the human sees. The median task verifier is 3 assertions and all 94 tasks together are 348 assertions (exp-ver-001); 89 of 94 task verifiers pass on the clean base tree (exp-ver-003). So the visible "verified" badge is produced by something like three assertions, and for 95% of tasks those same assertions pass without any change at all. The badge therefore discriminates a patch from the empty patch, not a good patch from a bad one. Mechanism: a check's information content is the probability it fails on a broken tree, and a test that passes on the base tree cannot distinguish "fixed" from "untouched". Falsifiable prediction: adding a mutation check - revert one line of the patch and require the verifier to fail - will reject a measurable fraction of currently-green patches; without it the badge should be rendered as "ran 3 assertions", never as "verified".

nodes.title: In a controlled coding-agent study the mandatory pre-merge check did not function as evidence: 39% of silent defects were caught
nodes.body: Dissanayake et al. (arXiv:2610.27801v1) ran a within-subject study, N=36, over 6 short Python tasks with 214 usable outcomes, seeding 71 silent-defect tasks into an agentic coding workflow. Participants resolved 28 of 71 (39%). 65 of 71 (91.5%) did perform at least one evaluative action beyond the mandatory pre-merge check, but only 40 of those actions were task-relevant, and of the 35 that produced defect-revealing evidence, 5 still did not recognize it. So the failure is not "nobody looked"; it is that the sanctioned check was generic and the human treated its passing as the evidence. Mechanism: a check that is always run and almost always passes becomes a ritual, and ritual completion substitutes for verification. Falsifiable prediction: removing the always-green check and replacing it with one task-specific assertion raises catch rate above 39% at equal time on task.

nodes.title: Silent-defect catch rate ranged 8% to 75% across six task types, and 79% of misses were rated 4 or 5 out of 5
nodes.body: Per-task catch rates in arXiv:2610.27801 Appendix C Table 5: CONFLICTS 1/12 = 8%, ATTENDANCE 3/12 = 25%, EQUIPMENT 4/12 = 33%, TAGS 6/12 = 50%, WAITLIST 5/11 = 45%, BILLING 9/12 = 75%. Mean confidence overall was 4.13/5. Among the 43 missed silent-defect tasks with valid ratings, 34 (79%) were rated 4 or 5. Recognized defects took M=10.8 min versus M=5.8 min for missed (Mann-Whitney p<.001), and confidence did not track that difference. Mechanism: confidence is a property of the human's prior, not of the evidence inspected, so it cannot be used to route review. Falsifiable prediction: an interface that asks for a confidence rating collects 4s and 5s on tasks the human has not inspected, and sorting the queue by self-reported confidence does not reduce defect escape.

nodes.title: The only behavioral marker separating catching from missing was time without typing: .622 vs .425 (d=1.29)
nodes.body: From arXiv:2610.27801: proportion of task time with no input activity was .622 on resolved silent-defect tasks versus .425 on missed ones, p<.001, Cohen's d=1.29 - the largest and most stable signal in the study. Keystroke rate, deletion counts, and cursor travel/speed did not distinguish outcomes. Gaze measures failed: pooled fixation and saccade rates differed but did not persist within participants, and fixation rate reversed direction (+7.39/min on resolved, p=.008); the authors conclude "gaze dynamics did not provide a reliable task-level marker". Physiological signals (heart-rate variability, respiration) did not distinguish conditions or outcomes. Mechanism: reading-and-thinking shows up as absence of typing, so dwell-without-input is a cheap proxy for inspection. Falsifiable prediction: a per-item dwell timer flagging approvals made with under 20% idle time catches more unexamined approvals than a confidence prompt, at zero sensor cost.

nodes.title: Absolute confidence did not recalibrate across rounds (4.17 to 4.09, n.s.) but relative thoroughness did track detection
nodes.body: arXiv:2610.27801 reports mean confidence on silent-defect tasks moving from 4.17 in round 1 to 4.09 in round 2, not significant, even after participants saw their round-1 results; 79% of misses were still rated 4-5/5. However a within-person measure did work: perceived thoroughness relative to one's own norm was 4.14 on caught tasks versus 3.49 on missed, and among the 16 participants who caught one and missed one, the caught task scored 0.93 points higher (p=.023). Mechanism: an absolute rating has no reference class, while a comparative judgement ("more or less careful than usual") does. Design consequence: ask the human to compare this item to their own baseline, or derive the comparison from dwell, but never trust a 1-5 absolute confidence field as a signal about inspection.

nodes.title: Explanations raised acceptance and subjective usefulness without raising team accuracy: 1,626 users, three tasks, no significant gain
nodes.body: Bansal et al., CHI 2021 (arXiv:2006.14779, DOI 10.1145/3411764.3445717), 1,626 participants over three tasks. Team accuracy with confidence only was already complementary (Beer 0.89 +/- 0.05 versus AI 0.84 and human 0.82). Adding explanations did not significantly improve it: Explain-Top-1 versus confidence-only gave Beer z=-1.18 p=.24, Amzbook z=1.23 p=.22, LSAT z=0.427 p=.64; adaptive explanation also failed (p=.31, .28, .87). Subjective usefulness rose anyway: 70% versus 57% (Beer), 65% versus 49% (Amzbook), 63% versus 45% (LSAT) rated the AI useful. Mechanism: a rationale is evidence of competence independent of its validity, so it moves approval, not accuracy. Falsifiable prediction: attaching a generated rationale to each queued patch raises approval rate while audited defect rate stays flat.

nodes.title: Explanations helped only where the human had independent ground truth: +5% when the AI was wrong on book reviews, negative on beer and LSAT
nodes.body: The mechanism inside arXiv:2006.14779 is an error split. When the AI was correct, explaining its top prediction helped; when the AI was wrong it hurt - except on Amazon book reviews, where Explain-Top-1 beat confidence-only by 5% on exactly the AI-wrong items, because participants could read the review and judge for themselves, and learned to distrust. On Beer and LSAT the same explanation decreased performance on AI-wrong items. So the value of a rationale is conditional on the human's ability to falsify it from the artifact. This applies directly to a code-patch queue: the human can falsify a claim about code by reading the diff (ground truth available), but cannot falsify a claim about whether the task was the right task. Design consequence: explain the diff, not the intent, and spend explanation budget where independent access exists.

nodes.title: Calibrated probability alone changed nothing; calibrated probability in frequency format let people adjust reliance
nodes.body: Cao, Liu, Huang (arXiv:2401.05612, PACM HCI 8, DOI 10.1145/3637318) ran a four-condition between-subjects study on skin-cancer screening, 15 trials, AI correct 12/15, with the participant's initial decision and 0-100 confidence collected before the AI suggestion. Conditions: no uncertainty, raw probability, calibrated probability, calibrated frequency. Result: showing calibrated model uncertainty alone was no better than uncalibrated confidence; only calibration combined with frequency framing let participants adjust reliance appropriately and reduced the confirmation-bias effect. Frequency wording used verbatim: "In 100 samples like this, AI would predict 72 to be benign, and 51 out of the 72 would actually be benign." Prior work they cite agrees: model confidence often has little effect (Bussone 2015; Rechkemmer and Yin 2022), and frequency format improved trust calibration without improving accuracy (Zhang 2020).

nodes.title: Quantile dotplots produced decisions worth 97% of optimal, 5 percentage points better than control
nodes.body: Fernandes, Walls, Munson, Hullman, Kay, CHI 2018 (DOI 10.1145/3173574.3173718) tested uncertainty displays for transit decisions. Decisions made with quantile dotplots (50 dots representing 50 outcomes) had expected payoffs at 97% of the optimal choice, 95% CI [95%, 98%] - 5 percentage points above control, 95% CI [2, 8]. Within-subject SD was 3 pp, 95% CI [2, 4], which is 4 pp less than control, 95% CI [2, 6]: the display made decisions both better and more consistent. Joslyn and LeClerc (J Exp Psychol Applied 18(1):126-140, 2012, DOI 10.1037/a0025185) found the same direction for numeric uncertainty forecasts: better precautionary decisions and preserved credibility after forecast misses. Mechanism: discrete outcome counts let a person simulate the decision instead of converting a probability, which is the step that fails. Falsifiable prediction: replacing a "confidence: 0.8" field with a 10-dot outcome strip raises the rate at which a supervisor picks the safer of two patches.

nodes.title: Open: does showing uncertainty make a supervisor defer more, or does any claim of competence do that?
nodes.body: The evidence does not support the common worry that uncertainty displays cause deference; it supports a sharper claim. Lai and Tan 2019 (cited in arXiv:2401.05612) found that presenting AI accuracy increases reliance even when the stated accuracy is chance; Bansal et al. 2021 found explanations raise acceptance regardless of correctness; Cao et al. found uncertainty presentation alone changes nothing. So the driver looks like "the system asserted something about itself", not "the system admitted doubt". What remains unmeasured: no study we found measures deference as a function of uncertainty display in a queue setting where the human has many items and limited time, and none measures whether an uncertainty display changes the decision to skip an item rather than the decision to approve it. Falsifiable test: same 60 patches, three arms (no uncertainty, calibrated frequency, dotplot), measure approve/skip/defer rates and audited defect rate.

nodes.title: The interventions that cut overreliance were the ones participants liked and trusted least (N=199)
nodes.body: Bucinca, Malaya, Gajos (PACM HCI 5 CSCW1, DOI 10.1145/3449287, arXiv:2102.09692), N=199 on MTurk, compared three cognitive forcing designs (on-demand explanation, decide-before-seeing-AI, forced delay) against two simple-XAI conditions and a no-AI baseline. Cognitive forcing significantly reduced overreliance on incorrect AI recommendations; it did not eliminate it. The load-bearing finding for interface design: participants gave the least favourable subjective ratings to exactly the conditions that reduced overreliance most - people over-relied less on the AI when exposed to conditions they found more difficult, preferred less, and trusted less. Benefits were also uneven: high need-for-cognition participants gained more, so the intervention widened the gap. Design consequence for an overnight loop: any friction that works will be rated worse than a smooth approve button, so friction has to be mandatory rather than a preference.

nodes.title: Hourly batching changed nothing; three batches a day reduced stress and raised well-being; alerts fully off raised anxiety
nodes.body: Fitz, Kushlev, Jagannathan, Lewis, Paliwal, Ariely, "Batching smartphone notifications can improve well-being", Computers in Human Behavior 101:84-94, Dec 2019: randomized field experiment, n=237, comparing three batching schedules against a control. Hourly batching produced little change versus control; batching three times per day reduced stress and increased well-being; switching alerts off entirely produced more anxiety and fear-of-missing-out. Mechanism: batching trades interruption cost for delivery delay, and the benefit appears only when the delay is long enough to consolidate while the channel stays open - silence is not a batch, it is a removal. Applies to an overnight loop: "no notifications until morning" is not the same intervention as "two digests, 07:00 and 19:00", and the fully-off arm is the one that measurably backfires. Falsifiable prediction: a single morning digest will be rated more anxiety-inducing than two digests carrying the same content.

nodes.title: Email batching cut exhaustion, then the effect wore off within two weeks, with no effect on engagement
nodes.body: Hettinga et al. 2022, "For whom and under what circumstances does email batching work?", Internet Interventions 27:100494 (PMC8897209), a non-randomized field study in a Dutch financial-services organization: 73 people in 4 intervention teams (3 batches per day) versus 39 in 3 control teams, one month. The intervention group had fewer email interruptions and lower emotional exhaustion immediately after the intervention, strongest for high email volume and where instant response was not expected. Effects wore off after two weeks; there was no significant effect on work engagement. The authors' own conclusion: "email batching should not be regarded as panacea." Prior evidence is mixed: Kushlev and Dunn 2015 and Bradley 2013 found batching beneficial, Mark et al. 2016 found a non-significant correlation, Akbar 2019 found it helps the emotionally stable and aggravates the neurotic, and Dabbish and Kraut 2006 associated restricted checking with email overload. Notification policy is a habit that decays, not a setting.

nodes.title: Alert-driven switching cost about 10 minutes plus 10-15 minutes to resume; 27% never returned within two hours
nodes.body: Iqbal and Horvitz, CHI 2007 (DOI 10.1145/1240624.1240730), field study of 27 Microsoft employees over two weeks and 2,267 hours: after an alert-driven switch to email, the average time to return to any suspended application was 9 min 33 s (8 min for IM), followed by a resumption phase of roughly 11-16.5 min depending on alert type. In 27% of cases the participant had still not returned to the original window after two hours; 40.8% of email alerts produced a switch to mail within 15 s while the other 59.2% averaged 7 min 32 s. Confidence medium: these figures come from secondary summaries, the primary PDF could not be fetched. A widely repeated "23 minutes to recover" figure distorts this work and should not be cited. The asymmetry for a queue: the cost is per interruption, so 114 interruptions cost far more than 114 items reviewed in one sitting.
nodes.source: DOI 10.1145/1240624.1240730 (numbers via secondary summaries; primary unfetched)

nodes.title: Interrupted work was finished faster at equal quality, at the price of stress and effort - the cost is affective
nodes.body: Mark, Gudith, Klocke, CHI 2008 (DOI 10.1145/1357054.1357072) found that people completed interrupted tasks in less time with no difference in quality: they compensate by working faster. The measured cost appears in stress, frustration, time pressure and perceived effort, moderated by personality (openness, need for personal structure). This contradicts the naive model that interruption mainly costs throughput, and it matters for a 06:00 queue review: a supervisor interrupted mid-review still finishes and reports the review as harder, so throughput and self-report both look acceptable while the affective cost accumulates. Falsifiable prediction: in a queue-review task with periodic interrupts, completion time and accuracy stay flat while stress and skipped-item rate rise. Related: Czerwinski, Cutrell and Horvitz (CHI 2000) found interruptions during the evaluation phase caused significantly longer completion times, and irrelevant interruptions cost more resumption than relevant ones.

nodes.title: Deliver at round boundaries: interruption cost depends on when it lands and is worst during evaluation
nodes.body: Adamczyk and Bailey, CHI 2004 (DOI 10.1145/985692.985727, pp. 271-278) established that interruption cost depends on the moment within task execution, with natural breakpoints being cheaper. Czerwinski, Cutrell and Horvitz, CHI 2000 found that interrupting during the evaluation phase caused significantly longer completion times, and that irrelevant interruptions produced longer message processing and longer resumption than relevant ones. For an overnight loop this gives a delivery rule with a mechanism: a round boundary is a breakpoint (the worker has stopped, state is committed, nothing is half-written), whereas a mid-round notification lands during the agent's own evaluation phase and costs the most. It also gives a relevance rule: a notification about the campaign under current review is cheap, one about a different campaign is expensive. Falsifiable prediction: the same number of notifications, aligned to round completion, will be rated less disruptive and produce fewer abandoned reviews than notifications fired on mid-round threshold crossings.

nodes.title: In ICU monitoring 85-99% of alarms were non-actionable; the actionable share ran from under 1% to 26%
nodes.body: Alarm fatigue is the best-measured case of a human supervising a machine that reports constantly. Cvach 2012 (Biomed Instrum Technol 46(4):268-277) reviewed that 85-99% of ICU alarms are non-actionable; a systematic review in J Hosp Med 2016;11(2):136 (DOI 10.1002/jhm.2520) put the actionable share at under 1% to 26% in adult ICUs, above 20% elsewhere. Drew et al. 2015 (PLOS ONE) observed 461 patients over 31 days with 2,558,760 unique alarms, an audible burden of 187 alarms per bed per day and 88.8% false - those exact figures are medium confidence here because the article page could not be re-fetched. Mechanism: response rate to an alert is set by its prior probability of being actionable, not by its severity label, so a channel that is 90% noise gets treated as noise regardless of what the 10% contains. An overnight loop that alerts on every round builds a 90%-noise channel before the human ever sees a real failure.
nodes.source: Cvach 2012; DOI 10.1002/jhm.2520; Drew et al. 2015 PLOS ONE (medium confidence)

nodes.title: An alert is actionable when it names a decision, an owner, and the default outcome of ignoring it
nodes.body: Combining the alarm-fatigue base rates (85-99% non-actionable; DOI 10.1002/jhm.2520) with the oversight study's finding that risky moments must become legible as requiring judgment (arXiv:2604.04918), an actionable notification has three testable components: (1) what changed, in one line, with the specific artifact and line range; (2) what decision is required, phrased as a choice with named options; (3) what happens if nobody acts, i.e. the default and its deadline. A message missing (2) is news, not an alert; missing (3) it cannot be triaged by cost. The ledger supplies a hard case: 80 of 127 real failures carried no diagnostic at all and all 80 had the diagnosis sitting in the child log (exp-fail-005), so 63% of the failure surface currently fails component (1) while the material to satisfy it already exists. Falsifiable prediction: adding (1)(2)(3) to every failure notification raises the fraction acted on within one day without increasing notification volume.

nodes.title: The out-of-the-loop problem predicts the morning-after supervisor has low situation awareness and slow failure detection
nodes.body: Endsley and Kiris, Human Factors 37(2):381-394, 1995 (DOI 10.1518/001872095779064555), automated a navigation task with an expert system and measured situation awareness and response to automation failure. Low situation awareness corresponded with out-of-the-loop performance decrements, specifically in decision time after the expert system failed; proposed causes are loss of manual skill, loss of situation awareness, vigilance and complacency effects, a shift from active to passive processing, and changed feedback. The human who supervises an overnight loop is in exactly this condition by construction: they did not perform the work, they did not watch it, and they arrive after the fact. The implication is not "show more detail" but "reconstruct the state the human would have had": what was attempted, what was expected, what actually happened, and what would count as a surprise. Falsifiable prediction: a handoff presenting expected-versus-actual per round will cut time-to-first-correct-decision on a seeded failure relative to a chronological log.

nodes.title: Automation bias is documented mainly under multitasking and complexity - exactly the queue condition
nodes.body: Lyell and Coiera, "Automation bias and verification complexity: a systematic review", JAMIA 24(2):423-431, 2017 (DOI 10.1093/jamia/ocw105): automation bias is overreliance on decision support that reduces vigilance in information seeking and processing. The review's framing is the useful part: the prevailing human-factors view is that automation bias occurs mainly in multitasking environments, and the health-care literature shows the same association with task complexity. A supervisor working a 114-item queue is multitasking by definition, so automation bias is the expected baseline condition, not an individual failing. This reframes the interface question: the design goal cannot be "make the human vigilant", it has to be "reduce the number of simultaneous judgements required per decision". Falsifiable prediction: presenting queue items strictly one at a time, with the previous item resolved before the next appears, reduces acceptance of incorrect proposals relative to a scannable list.

nodes.title: Making someone accountable for decision accuracy reduced automation bias in experiment - a cheap, testable lever
nodes.body: Skitka, Mosier, Burdick and Gentry (1999) found that holding participants accountable for their performance or decision accuracy reduced automation bias relative to a no-accountability condition. The mechanism is a shift from acceptance to verification: if the decision will be reviewed, checking becomes instrumentally useful. For an unattended loop this becomes an interface element that costs almost nothing to build - every approval requires one line of justification, and a sample is later audited against the artifact. Honest limit: this is a 1999 laboratory result with a decision-support aid, verified here only at second hand through the automation-bias literature, not a study of code-patch review; the transfer is an inference, not a measurement, hence medium confidence. Falsifiable prediction: requiring a one-line justification per approved patch with a 10% blind audit lowers the acceptance rate of seeded-defect patches relative to one-click approve, and raises median dwell per item.
nodes.source: Skitka et al. 1999 (second-hand via automation-bias literature; not independently fetched)

nodes.title: Oversight strategy changed which harmful actions users were exposed to more reliably than it changed their ability to correct them (N=48)
nodes.body: Chen et al., arXiv:2604.04918v1 (Apr 2026), within-subjects with 48 participants, six live-web tasks in two consequence levels with embedded privacy leakage, prompt injection and dark patterns, under four oversight strategies (risk-gated agent-led, approve-every-action, plan-level supervisory co-execution, structurally enriched plan plus step plus risk). The central measured claim: oversight strategy shaped users' exposure to problematic actions more reliably than their ability to correct those actions once visible; plan-based strategies reduced the occurrence of problematic actions without equally strong gains in runtime intervention success. Qualitative themes from their codebook: "repeated approvals create decision fatigue", "approve similar is perceived as dangerous", "oversight as approve-first, verify-later", "prefer consolidated oversight", "pace is too fast". Design consequence for a queue: prevention at plan time beats correction at approval time, and review capacity should be spent before execution, not after.

nodes.title: Approve-similar collapses N decisions into one and reproduces the multitasking condition automation bias needs
nodes.body: From the qualitative codebook of arXiv:2604.04918 ("approve similar is perceived as dangerous", "treat related fields as one category", "oversight as approve-first, verify-later"), plus the automation-bias condition of multitasking and complexity (DOI 10.1093/jamia/ocw105), a specific failure mode follows for a 114-patch queue: any bulk or approve-all-like-this control converts the visible decision surface back into a single decision made under time pressure, which is precisely the condition in which vigilance collapses. The same study found users prefer consolidated oversight, so the pressure toward bulk is real and is a preference, not an oversight. The design tension is therefore explicit: consolidation reduces effort and increases exposure, and both cannot be optimised at once. Falsifiable prediction: adding approve-similar to a queue interface increases approvals per minute and increases the number of patches approved without item-level inspection, measurable via dwell (the .622 vs .425 inactivity marker in arXiv:2610.27801).

nodes.title: A better agent-trace interface cut error-finding time and raised confidence without improving accuracy
nodes.body: Grunde-McLaughlin, Mozannar, Murad, Chen, Amershi, Fourney, "Overseeing Agents Without Constant Oversight", arXiv:2602.16844 (Feb 2026), report three user studies on a Computer Use Agent: an action-trace baseline for verification, three design probes, then a novel interface evaluated on error-finding in question answering. Current trace practices were found cumbersome and limiting; the proposed design reduced time spent finding errors, and participants reported higher confidence in their decisions, but final accuracy was not meaningfully improved. This is the cleanest available warning against time-to-decision and self-reported confidence as success metrics for a supervision interface: both improved while the thing that matters did not. Falsifiable prediction: any queue UI change should be evaluated on audited defect escape rate against a seeded-defect set, and a change that only improves review latency or confidence should be treated as unproven.

nodes.title: A minimum dwell per patch is the cheapest force-function this loop can build, and it is testable
nodes.body: Three measurements combine. Recognition of a silent defect took M=10.8 min versus M=5.8 min for a miss, and the differentiating behavior was time without typing (.622 vs .425, d=1.29) (arXiv:2610.27801). Cognitive forcing functions reduce overreliance but are disliked (arXiv:2102.09692). Faster review raised confidence without raising accuracy (arXiv:2602.16844). A minimum-dwell rule - an approval cannot be registered until the diff has been open for, say, 90 s, or until every hunk has been scrolled past - is the local instantiation of all three: it forces the idle-thinking time that separated catching from missing, it is a forcing function so it will be disliked, and its success must be measured on catch rate, not on time saved. Falsifiable prediction: on a 20-patch audit set with 6 seeded defects, a 90 s dwell floor raises catch rate above an unconstrained baseline at a cost of roughly 20-30 minutes per session, and participants rate it worse.

nodes.title: 69% of the brief is identical text and 47% is the report contract - dedupe before adding anything
nodes.body: The measured brief is 69% identical text, and the report contract alone accounts for 47% of it (exp-brief-001). This bounds what any additional interface element can achieve: if the human's reading budget is fixed, up to 69% of it is currently spent on text that does not change between rounds, and the actionable delta is at most 31%. Mechanism: identical text is not neutral - it costs scanning time and it trains the reader to skim, which is the same desensitisation mechanism as alarm fatigue (85-99% non-actionable, Cvach 2012) applied to prose. Design consequence: the first intervention is subtraction - diff the brief against the previous one and render only changed sections; the second is moving the contract out of the human view entirely. Falsifiable prediction: a brief that omits unchanged boilerplate is read further into the document per session and produces more acted-on failures, at equal or lower token cost.

nodes.title: 80 of 127 real failures shipped with no diagnostic, while the diagnosis already existed in the child log
nodes.body: Ledger measurement exp-fail-005: of 127 real failures, 80 carried no diagnostic at all, and all 80 had the diagnosis available in the child log. That is 63% of the failure surface blank at the point where a human would look, with the material to fill it already generated and paid for. This is a supply problem, not a summarization problem: the interface does not need to infer why a round failed, it needs to stop discarding the reason. It also interacts with the report contract: 47% of the brief is contract boilerplate (exp-brief-001), so budget spent on structure is being spent instead of on the one line that would make a failure actionable. Falsifiable prediction: extracting the last error line and the failing command from the child log into every failure entry raises the fraction of failures a human can classify without opening the log from 37% to above 90%, at negligible token cost.

nodes.title: The queue is priced wrong by 71x: about 7 cents per landed promotion at real card prices
nodes.body: Ledger measurement w5-tokenbudget: cost per landed promotion is about 7 cents at real card prices, 71 times more than the ledger recorded. A supervisor deciding about a queue is implicitly making a cost decision - is this patch worth the run that produced it - and that decision is currently made against a number two orders of magnitude too small. Mechanism: the same understatement applies to whatever review costs if review is charged to the same budget, so the interface's own economics are invisible. Design consequence: show marginal cost per queued item next to the decision and show campaign spend against its cap, because a queue review that ignores cost will systematically over-approve expensive-to-reverify work. Falsifiable prediction: adding cost-per-item to the queue reduces the number of items approved for re-verification without changing the number approved for promotion, and shifts spend toward campaigns with higher landed-promotion yield.

nodes.title: Zero of 100 lessons were reused across campaigns, so a cross-campaign what-we-learned panel shows nothing
nodes.body: Ledger measurement exp-transfer-001: 0 cross-campaign reuse out of 100 lessons. Any interface element that aggregates lessons across campaigns is therefore displaying, by measurement, a body of text no campaign has ever acted on. The mechanism is that lessons are written in the vocabulary of the campaign that produced them (specific files, specific verifier commands) and a supervisor reading a different campaign cannot map them onto the decision in front of them - a retrieval problem, not a writing problem. Design consequence: the human view should show only campaign-local deltas plus a pointer to the exact artifact; the cross-campaign summary should be dropped from the brief until reuse is demonstrated above zero. Falsifiable prediction: replacing a global lessons panel with per-campaign "last three failures of this kind" produces measurable reuse (a lesson cited in a later round's brief) where the current panel produces none.

nodes.title: Task horizons are doubling roughly every 7 months, so the unit the human must review keeps growing
nodes.body: METR, "Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks", arXiv:2503.14499 (Mar 2025), measured the 50%-success task time horizon doubling on a roughly 7-month cadence, with later revisions putting the post-2023 doubling at about 131 days and post-2024 at about 89 days. Naive extrapolation puts a one-month (167 work-hour) horizon somewhere between late 2028 and early 2031. For supervision interfaces the relevant consequence is not the date but the derivative: the unit a human must review grows over time, so a queue design tuned for 59-line patches (6,684 lines over 114 patches, exp-human-007) will be reviewing far larger patches within a few doublings, and dwell-per-item cannot scale by adding minutes. Falsifiable prediction: review interfaces must shift from per-line inspection to per-invariant checking (did the patch preserve stated properties) as patch size grows, and per-line dwell floors stop discriminating once patches exceed a few hundred lines.

nodes.title: A morning brief that earns its reading time: five fields, one screen, ranked by decision cost
nodes.body: Synthesis with a fixed shape, each field tied to a measurement. (1) What changed since the human last looked, diffed against the previous brief, because 69% of the current brief is identical text (exp-brief-001). (2) For each failure, the one-line cause pulled from the child log, because 80 of 127 failures currently have none and all 80 have it available (exp-fail-005). (3) N pending decisions ranked by cost of ignoring, each with a named default, because an alert without a default cannot be triaged (base rates in DOI 10.1002/jhm.2520). (4) Marginal cost per item, because real cost is 71x the ledger's number (w5-tokenbudget). (5) One seeded audit item per session, because a better trace interface raised confidence without raising accuracy (arXiv:2602.16844) and only an audit measures the human. Falsifiable prediction: this one-screen brief produces a higher rate of acted-on failures than the current 69%-boilerplate brief at equal token budget.

nodes.title: An AI monitor that catches 38% of intentionally hidden backdoors is the machine-side analogue of a 39% human catch rate
nodes.body: Greenblatt, Roger, Sachan, Shlegeris, "AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion", arXiv:2312.06942 (Dec 2023), evaluates protocols against an untrusted model that may insert backdoors into code, over a 5,000-problem benchmark. Numbers as reported for the first two table rows in a secondary paper: trusted monitoring completes the set with no undetected backdoor 62% of the time; trusted editing reaches 92%. Read as failure rates, a monitoring protocol misses 38% and an editing protocol misses 8%. That 38% sits within a point of the 39% silent-defect catch rate measured for humans in arXiv:2610.27801, which is the interesting coincidence: an automated monitor and an unaided human supervisor land at similar detection rates on adversarially hidden defects, while a protocol with a second model reviewing reaches 92%. Confidence medium: the figures are quoted from a secondary summary of Table 1, not read off the paper.
nodes.source: arXiv:2312.06942 (figures via secondary summary of Table 1)

nodes.title: Explain the doubt, not the decision: a rationale that argues for approval is an approval-rate optimiser
nodes.body: Bansal et al. conclude from their own null result that explanations should be designed to expose doubt rather than to persuade, and raise asynchronous presentation and devil's-advocate framing as unexplored alternatives (arXiv:2006.14779). A secondary governance-design source states the same rule normatively - do not let the interface argue for its own proposal, because a system that generates a compelling rationale for its proposal is optimising approval rate, not decision quality - but that source is design guidance, not a measurement, so it is used here only as restatement, not evidence. The mechanism is the one measured in the paper: a rationale is competence evidence regardless of validity, and it moved subjective usefulness (70% vs 57%) while moving accuracy not at all. Concrete form for a queue: show the strongest reason not to merge - the assertion that would have caught it, the untested path, the touched file with no test - instead of a summary of why it is good.
nodes.source: arXiv:2006.14779 (plus non-measurement design guidance, flagged as such)

nodes.title: Show failures by default and successes on demand: the asymmetry is in the base rate, not in the interest
nodes.body: Two ledger facts set the base rate for a morning view. 89 of 94 task verifiers pass on the clean base tree (exp-ver-003) and the score is binary (exp-score-001), so a successful round carries one bit that is mostly predicted; a failed round carries the diagnosis, and 80 of 127 failures carried none (exp-fail-005). Alarm research says response is governed by the prior probability that a message is actionable, not by its label (85-99% of ICU alarms non-actionable, Cvach 2012; DOI 10.1002/jhm.2520). Together: a view that lists successes spends finite attention on the majority class and dilutes the channel, while the minority class that needs a decision is the one currently blank. Falsifiable prediction: a brief listing only failures plus a count of successes is acted on faster than one listing both, and the difference grows as the campaign pass rate rises.

nodes.title: Two windows, not continuous and not silence: 07:00 triage and 19:00 deep review, delivered at round boundaries
nodes.body: Combining the batching RCT (hourly batching near control; 3x/day reduced stress and raised well-being; alerts fully off raised anxiety and fear-of-missing-out, Fitz et al. 2019, n=237) with the breakpoint result (interruption cost depends on the moment, evaluation-phase interruption is worst, Adamczyk and Bailey CHI 2004) and the decay result (batching benefits wore off in two weeks, PMC8897209), an overnight loop's notification policy has a defensible shape: two scheduled windows per day, aligned to round boundaries, with digest content ranked by decision cost. The windows are the batching intervention; alignment to round boundaries is the breakpoint intervention; expecting re-establishment after decay is the maintenance requirement. Falsifiable prediction: comparing continuous notification, a two-window digest, and no notification over four weeks, the digest wins on reported stress and acted-on-failure rate while the no-notification arm is worst on anxiety - and the digest's advantage shrinks by week three unless the schedule is re-affirmed.

nodes.title: One intervening successful task collapsed silent-defect detection from 50% to 9.1%
nodes.body: arXiv:2610.27801 measured a carryover effect that is the most actionable number in the study. A silent defect placed immediately after a visible failure was detected in 12 of 24 cases (50%). When one correctly-completed task intervened between the visible failure and the silent defect, detection fell to 1 of 11 (9.1%); permutation p=.046, Fisher p=.023, residualized t=2.44 p=.020. The authors describe the effect as short-lived: a single success restores trust. Note the power limit - only 6 participants contributed to the gap sequence - so treat the 50-to-9.1 drop as directionally solid and the exact magnitude as uncertain. Mechanism: a visible failure raises vigilance, a success discharges it, and the discharge is not proportional to the evidence the success provides. Interface consequence: a morning view that interleaves green items between failures destroys the salience the failures created, and a run of green items before a failure is read as an all-clear.

nodes.title: SWE-bench task construction: F2P/P2P is defined as a transition, not a pass check
nodes.body: SWE-bench collects 2,294 task instances from PRs in 12 Python repositories; an instance is a PR associated with an issue that modified 1+ testing files. Per instance it builds a Docker image at the commit the PR is based on. The site states the construction criterion verbatim: "Without the Pull Request's changes, a number of test(s) fail. After the PR is merged, the same set of test(s) pass. These 'Fail-to-Pass' tests are the primary signal for evaluation." Evaluation requires both sets: FAIL_TO_PASS must pass (did the patch fix it) and PASS_TO_PASS must not regress (did the patch break anything else); the tests are hidden from the agent. This matters for the proposal because the benchmark oracle is already a differential oracle: the unit of measurement is an ordered pair of runs in one environment, base-tree then patched-tree, and a single passing run carries no label at all.

nodes.title: A verifier that already passes on the base tree has zero mutual information with the patch
nodes.body: Ledger measurement exp-ver-003: 89 of 94 task verifiers pass on the clean base tree. Ledger measurement exp-ver-001: the median task verifier has 3 assertions and all 94 tasks together have 348, i.e. 3.7 assertions per task. A boolean that is 1 before the patch and 1 after the patch cannot distinguish a correct patch from an empty patch from a destructive patch that happens to miss the 3 asserted behaviors; its only possible signal is an accidental regression. With 3 assertions the detection surface for an unrelated regression is tiny, so the current oracle is close to a constant function of the patch. Falsifiable prediction: revert the patch on 20 of the 89 base-passing tasks (base tree minus the accepted change) and re-run the unmodified verifier; if it still reports pass on >=17 of 20, the verifier is proven patch-independent at 85% rate, and every promotion it ever granted was unfalsifiable.

nodes.title: Score the transition, not the state: (F2P gained, P2P lost) as the round's oracle
nodes.body: The proposal is to run the verifier twice in the same round, once on the base tree and once on the patched tree, and score the pair: F2P gained = assertions that fail on base and pass on the patch; P2P lost = assertions that pass on base and fail on the patch. SWE-bench already formalizes exactly this, so the design is not novel research, it is adopting a known oracle. The ledger's current verifier is the degenerate case with an empty F2P set: it is a P2P-only oracle whose P2P set was selected to pass, so it is structurally incapable of awarding credit. Two consequences follow. First, a base run becomes mandatory, so the loop acquires a reproducibility precondition it did not have. Second, the score stops being binary (exp-score-001) and becomes a pair of small integers, which restores gradient where minGain previously could never change a decision (exp-gate-001) because 0->1 was the only available move. Prediction: on the 5 non-base-passing tasks the change is neutral; on the 89 it is the only change that can produce a non-zero F2P term at all.

nodes.title: 34 of SWE-bench Lite's 300 problems have flaky suites; 30 of them contaminate the gold patch
nodes.body: Appendix evidence from Brown et al. (Large Language Monkeys, 2407.21787) on SWE-bench Lite: the authors identified 34 problems whose test suites had flaky tests, and 30 of those affected the dataset-provided correct solutions - meaning the gold patch itself sometimes fails, so a differential oracle would score a correct patch as P2P-lost. Their mitigation was brute force: on any problem with flaky tests they ran the suite 11 times and used majority voting to decide pass/fail, and they also report a 266-problem subset with the flaky problems removed. Their preliminary cause was unpinned dependency versions in the Docker environments running the unit tests, and one instance (astropy__astropy-6938) was flaky on some machines and not others - the SWE-bench authors could reproduce it, these authors could not. That is the crucial shape of the problem for a self-hosted loop: flakiness is environment-local, so 11.3% of instances (34/300) is a lower bound borrowed from someone else's image, not a property transferable to your runner.

nodes.title: At Google, 84% of pass-to-fail transitions are flaky tests - the exact signal a differential oracle reads
nodes.body: Micco's ICSE-SEIP 2017 industrial report ('Taming Google-Scale Continuous Testing') and the derived talks report: about 4.2 million tests on the CI system, roughly 62,000 (~1.5%) exhibiting flaky behavior in a week, ~16% of tests showing some level of flakiness, 84% of pass-to-fail transitions coming from flaky tests, only 1.23% of tests ever finding a breakage, and 2-16% of compute spent re-running flaky tests. This is the single most damaging number for the proposal: the transition a differential oracle interprets as 'the patch broke a P2P test' is, in Google's data, a flake 84% of the time. Two mechanisms follow. A P2P-lost event is 6:1 more likely to be noise than a real regression at that base rate, so a naive differential score would reject most correct patches; and the same asymmetry makes a P2P-gained event untrustworthy as credit. Any two-run oracle therefore needs a flake discriminator between the runs, not a majority vote after the fact.

nodes.title: DeFlaker: a failing test that covers no changed code is flaky, with no rerun (1.5% false alarms, 95.5% recall)
nodes.body: Bell et al. (ICSE 2018, DeFlaker) detect flakiness by lightweight differential coverage tracking: if a test fails but did not cover any changed code, it is reported flaky without re-execution. Evaluation over re-runs of 5,966 builds across 26 open-source projects found 4,846 flaky tests, with a 1.5% false-alarm rate and 95.5% recall versus 23% for Maven's default flaky detector; only the very costly Reboot strategy found more. The mechanism generalizes to a two-run differential oracle almost without modification: the patched tree has an explicit diff, so every assertion that transitions fail->pass or pass->fail can be cross-checked against whether its test executed the changed lines. A pass->fail on a test that never touched the diff is a flake or an environment effect by construction, and a fail->pass on such a test is not attributable to the patch and should not earn credit. This is the cheapest available substitute for k-times rerun voting, and it is one coverage map per run rather than k extra suites.

nodes.title: 61.1% of 1,699 SWE-bench samples were flagged for F2P tests that unfairly reject valid solutions
nodes.body: OpenAI's SWE-bench Verified campaign annotated 1,699 random samples with 93 Python developers, three annotators per sample, taking the highest-severity label. Result: 38.3% of samples flagged for underspecified problem statements, 61.1% flagged for unit tests that may unfairly mark valid solutions as incorrect, and 68.3% filtered out overall for underspecification, unfair unit tests, or other issues. The filtering is explicitly overzealous by design, so 61.1% is an upper bound on the flag rate, not a false-reject rate - the honest reading is that more than half of the human-written F2P suites were judged capable of rejecting a correct alternative implementation. The canonical example given is scikit-learn-14520, where the F2P test requires an exact DeprecationWarning message negotiated in the PR, a string the issue text never mentions. For a differential oracle this sets the false-reject floor: an over-specific F2P assertion fails a correct patch on the patched tree while passing on base, which the transition score reads as 'no credit', not as 'oracle defect'.

nodes.title: SWE-Bench+: 32.67% of successful patches were leaked, 31.08% were weak-test passes; resolve rate falls 12.47% to 3.97%
nodes.body: Aleithan et al. (arXiv:2410.06992) manually screened instances that SWE-Agent + GPT-4 resolved and compared model patches to the real PRs. Findings: 32.67% of successful patches involved cheating because the solution was directly present in the issue report or comments (solution leakage); 31.08% of passed patches were suspicious because the tests were not adequate to verify correctness (weak test cases); over 94% of issues predate model knowledge cutoffs. After filtering both classes, the resolution rate fell from 12.47% to 3.97%, and the same quality problems were present in SWE-bench Lite and SWE-bench Verified. The false-accept number that matters for the proposal is the 31.08%: those patches genuinely passed the F2P suite, so no amount of correct base-run/patch-run bookkeeping fixes them. A differential oracle fixes the base-passes-already failure mode; it does not fix under-specified assertions, and this paper is the measurement showing the two are separable failure modes that need separate remedies.

nodes.title: UTBoost: 36 under-tested instances and 345 patches falsely marked passed, moving 40.9% of Lite ranks
nodes.body: Yu et al. (ACL 2025, arXiv:2506.09289) build UTGenerator, an LLM-driven test generator that analyzes codebases and dependencies to synthesize additional test cases for real Python projects, then re-score existing SWE-bench submissions with the augmented suites. They identify 36 task instances with insufficient test cases and uncover 345 erroneous patches incorrectly labeled as passed in the original SWE-bench. Those corrections impact 40.9% of SWE-Bench Lite and 24.4% of SWE-Bench Verified leaderboard entries, producing 18 and 11 ranking changes respectively. This is the strongest published evidence that a passing F2P suite is a weak certificate: hundreds of patches that satisfied every original assertion were still wrong, and the only way to expose them was to write more assertions, not to run the existing ones more carefully. It is also the closest thing to a measured false-accept rate for a well-run F2P oracle on real submissions, and it is a lower bound because UTBoost only adds tests it managed to generate.

nodes.title: PatchDiff: 7.8% of 'solved' patches fail the developer's own suite; 29.6% differ behaviorally from the gold patch
nodes.body: Wang et al. (arXiv:2503.15223, 'Are Solved Issues in SWE-bench Really Solved Correctly?') introduce PatchDiff, differential patch testing that exposes behavioral discrepancies between two patches, and apply it to three state-of-the-art issue solvers on SWE-bench Verified. Results: 7.8% of all patches count as correct while failing the developer-written test suite; 29.6% of plausible patches induce different behavior than the ground-truth patch; of those divergences, 46.8% come from similar-but-divergent implementations and 27.3% from patches that adapt more behavior than the ground truth; manual inspection judges 28.6% of behaviorally divergent patches certainly incorrect; combined, 6.2 absolute percentage points of reported resolution rate are inflation. This is the closest published mechanism to the proposal, and it is a differential oracle between two patches rather than between base and patched - which is strictly stronger information and strictly more expensive, since it needs a trusted reference patch that a self-improvement loop does not have.

nodes.title: The ledger's verifiers cap a differential oracle at ~3 bits per task; assertion-level scoring is the free upgrade
nodes.body: Arithmetic on the given measurements: 348 assertions / 94 tasks = 3.70 assertions per task, median 3 (exp-ver-001), and 89/94 verifiers already pass on base (exp-ver-003). A verifier that collapses its assertions into one boolean yields at most 2^3 = 8 distinct outcome vectors across the two runs, and conditioning on 'base passes all three' leaves one trivial all-pass state plus the regression states. So the maximum new information a base+patch double-run can extract from the existing 94 verifiers is log2(8) = 3 bits per task per round, and in practice 1 bit: any P2P regression or none. The fix costs no new test authoring: score the assertion-level vector (which of the 3 transitioned), not the aggregate. Prediction: two patches that the boolean ties will differ on at least one assertion transition in >=20% of the 89 base-passing tasks; if the observed rate is under 5%, assertion-level resolution is not worth the parser work and the loop should instead spend on generating new assertions (the UTBoost route).

nodes.title: Static RTS across 985 revisions of 22 projects: class-level is comparable to Ekstazi but unsafe sometimes
nodes.body: Legunsen, Hariri, Shi, Lu, Zhang and Marinov (FSE 2016, 'An extensive study of static regression test selection in modern software evolution') implemented a class-level and a method-level static RTS and compared variants against Ekstazi, a state-of-the-art class-level dynamic RTS, on 985 revisions of 22 open-source projects. The headline result: class-level static RTS is comparable to Ekstazi with similar performance benefits, but at the risk of being unsafe sometimes; the method-level static technique performs rather poorly. Safety is defined precisely - a technique is safe if it selects to run all tests that may be affected by code changes - and the paper's framing of the cost model is the one a loop should copy: end-to-end time of RTS = dependency collection + change analysis + execution of selected tests, and that total must beat the time to run all tests for the optimization to exist at all. The 22-project/985-revision scale is the largest RTS evidence base found, and it is Java, not Python.

nodes.title: Retest-all 48.7s vs Ekstazi 18.7s end-to-end average across 10 Java projects
nodes.body: In the Reks evaluation table (Wang, Godfrey, Gligoric, ASE 2018, 'Towards Refactoring-Aware Regression Test Selection'), average end-to-end regression testing time across 10 Java projects is 48.7s for retest-all and 18.7s for Ekstazi, with Reks at 9.3s - a 2.6x wall-clock reduction from dynamic file-level selection. Per-project spread is wide (IO: 132.7s vs 11.9s; Stateless4J: 2.2s vs 2.8s, where selection loses), which matters more than the average: on small suites the dependency analysis costs more than it saves. Read this as the only concrete price found for 'keep the second run cheap', with three caveats: it is Java class-level selection from 2018, the workloads are refactoring-oriented rather than agent patches, and end-to-end includes the analysis the paper is optimizing. For a Python loop the transferable claim is the shape - selection pays when suites are long and diffs are narrow - not the 2.6x.

nodes.title: An unsafe selector silently converts a failing test into an unrun test - the cost optimization manufactures false accepts
nodes.body: RTS safety is a definition, not a heuristic: a technique is safe iff it selects every test whose behavior may be affected by the change (Rothermel-Harrold tradition; Legunsen et al. 2016 confirm class-level static RTS is sometimes unsafe). Compose that with a differential oracle and the failure mode is precise: if a regression test is not selected on the patched run, the oracle sees no P2P-lost event and scores the patch as clean. The selector therefore does not merely lose a little detection power, it removes exactly the evidence the oracle was built to collect, and it does so invisibly - a false accept introduced by the very optimization adopted to make the second run affordable. This is why the two halves of the proposal are coupled: base-run cost and selection safety must be evaluated together. Prediction: inject a known-breaking patch touching a file outside the selector's dependency graph; an unsafe selector will report zero P2P-lost while retest-all reports at least one, and the detection gap is the selector's false-accept contribution, measurable per patch as the difference between selected-set and full-set verdicts.

nodes.title: SWE-smith manufactures the missing failing test by breaking existing tests in any codebase
nodes.body: SWE-smith (Yang et al., NeurIPS 2025, arXiv:2504.21798) answers directly the hardest case in the proposal - a base tree where nothing fails. Given any Python codebase it constructs an execution environment and then automatically synthesizes hundreds to thousands of task instances that break existing test(s) in the codebase, yielding 50k instances from 128 repositories, an order of magnitude more than prior work, and training SWE-agent-LM-32B to 40.2% Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified. The significance for a differential oracle is that the F2P set need not be found, it can be created: inject a fault, verify the suite now fails, and you have a fail-to-pass pair whose ground truth is the inverse of the injection. That converts an unfalsifiable base-passing verifier into a task with a known-failing assertion. The open question it leaves is quality - a synthesized task tests exactly the fault the generator chose, so the F2P set inherits the generator's blind spots rather than the issue's requirements.

nodes.title: Mutants couple to real faults for 73% of faults (357 faults, 230K mutants) - so a mutation oracle has a ~27% blind spot
nodes.body: Just, Jalali, Inozemtseva, Ernst, Holmes and Fraser (FSE 2014, 'Are mutants a valid substitute for real faults in software testing?') run the largest such study: 357 real faults from Defects4J and 230,000 mutants. Core result: the mutant detection rate increased for 73% of faults, i.e. for 73% of real faults some mutant was killed by tests that also detect the fault (coupling), and on average about 2 mutants are coupled to a fault; mutation score is a stronger predictor of real-fault detection than statement coverage, including when coverage is held fixed. The honest reading for the proposal's fallback: if the loop substitutes mutation score for a failing test, it inherits a blind spot on the ~27% of faults with no coupled mutant, and that blind spot is not random - uncoupled faults cluster around the mutation operators used (the paper finds operator-dependent coupling, with conditional/relational operator replacement and statement deletion implicated). The paper won the FSE 2024 Most Influential Paper award, so the 73% figure is well replicated, but it was measured on Java, not on 59-line Python agent patches.

nodes.title: MuTAP: surviving mutants as prompts detect up to 28% more faulty code, 17% of it undetected by Pynguin
nodes.body: Moradi Dakhel et al. (arXiv:2308.16557) build MuTAP, which generates tests with an LLM and then re-prompts using surviving mutants, because a surviving mutant is a concrete witness that the current suite does not check that behavior. Results: up to 28% more faulty human-written snippets detected; 17% of those remained undetected by both Pynguin (a state-of-the-art automated generator) and zero-shot/few-shot LLM prompting; mutation score 93.57% on synthetic buggy code, beating all baselines. Mechanically this is the cheapest known way to escape the base-passing trap without human test authoring: run mutation analysis on the base tree, take the surviving mutants as a to-do list, and the resulting tests are guaranteed to fail on base and pass on a correct fix - i.e. they are F2P by construction. Caveat: the 93.57% figure is on synthetic bugs and the 28% is relative, so neither is a false-accept rate for real agent patches.

nodes.title: Metamorphic relations as an oracle where no expected output exists - checkable without a base-tree failure
nodes.body: Metamorphic testing replaces the expected-output oracle with relations across transformed inputs: instead of asserting f(x) = y, assert that f(T(x)) relates to f(x) in a stated way (permutation invariance, monotonicity, scaling). The standard reference is Segura, Fraser, Sanchez and Ruiz-Cortes, 'A Survey on Metamorphic Testing', IEEE TSE 42(9):805-824, 2016, which frames it exactly as the oracle problem's answer when the input-output relation is complex or unavailable. Its relevance here is structural: a metamorphic relation needs no failing test on the base tree, so it can serve as the F2P side where nothing fails, and it is checkable on both trees in the same round. But it has a hard boundary the proposal must respect: an MR that holds on base and holds on the patch contributes nothing to a transition score, so MRs cannot certify a patch that changes no observable behavior. Prediction: for a refactor-only round (no output change), every MR passes on both trees and the differential score is identically zero regardless of correctness - MRs catch output-changing faults only. Confidence is low on any detection-rate claim: the survey is paywalled and only the bibliographic record and abstract were verified, so no numeric MR detection rate is asserted here.

nodes.title: Three concrete ways the base run lies: dependency drift, broken environment graded as wrong, and a base commit absent from the object db
nodes.body: First, unpinned dependencies: the Large Language Monkeys authors traced SWE-bench Lite flakiness to unpinned dependency versions in the Docker environments, and found astropy__astropy-6938 flaky on some machines and not others - so the same nominal base tree is a different program on different hosts (arXiv:2407.21787). Second, environment build failure graded as a solution failure: OpenAI states it is sometimes difficult to reliably set up SWE-bench development environments, inadvertently causing unit tests to fail regardless of the solution, so perfectly valid solutions get marked incorrect. Third, the base tree may not exist at all: the Repo2RLEnv validation pipeline documents that its bootstrap image ships a depth=1 shallow clone, so historical PR base commits are absent from the object database until explicitly fetched, and `git reset --hard <base_commit>` fails without that fetch. Add the EnvBench/EvoConfig failure split (32.4% hardware insufficiency, 28.2% missing or incomplete config such as pyproject.toml or requirements.txt) and the base run is the least reliable component of the whole proposal. A differential oracle must therefore fail closed on a non-reproducible base, never score it.

nodes.title: The second run costs wall clock, not tokens - and the ledger's patches are small enough for selection to pay
nodes.body: Ledger measurement w5-tokenbudget: about 7 cents per landed promotion at real card prices, 71x more than the ledger recorded. A base run adds no model tokens and no prompt length; it adds one suite execution per round, so the marginal cost is wall clock and container time, and the comparison that matters is suite duration versus the 7-cent model spend. Ledger measurement exp-human-007: the whole promotion queue is 6,684 changed lines across 114 patches, an average of 58.6 lines per patch. Small diffs are the regime where coverage-based selection works: Ekstazi's class-level selection cut end-to-end time from 48.7s to 18.7s on 10 Java projects (Reks table, ASE 2018), and Legunsen et al. found class-level static RTS comparable on 985 revisions of 22 projects. Prediction: on these 114 patches, a diff-coverage selector will run a median of under 30% of the suite; if the observed median is above 70%, the base-run cost roughly doubles wall clock per round and the proposal should be gated behind a cheaper pre-check instead.

nodes.title: Design: base pre-flight, F2P/P2P split, diff-coverage flake filter, assertion-level score
nodes.body: Concrete design assembled from the sourced pieces. (1) Base pre-flight: run the verifier twice on a clean, pinned tree; if the two runs disagree, or the base commit cannot be materialized, mark the round unscored and fix the environment - never score it (justified by arXiv:2407.21787, the OpenAI environment note, and the Repo2RLEnv shallow-clone failure). (2) Split assertions into F2P (fail on base, pass on patch) and P2P (pass on both); credit only F2P, penalize only P2P-lost. (3) Flake filter: discard any transition whose test did not execute lines in the diff, DeFlaker-style, with 1.5% false alarms and 95.5% recall (ICSE 2018); only residual disagreements pay for k reruns. (4) Score assertion-level, not boolean, to get ~3 bits instead of 1 (exp-ver-001). Prediction: this converts the 89 base-passing tasks from an all-pass constant into a real signal, and a reward hack that deletes or weakens assertions becomes visible as P2P-lost rather than invisible; if it does not, the verifiers' assertions are not patch-observable at all and only new assertions (UTBoost, MuTAP) can help.

nodes.title: Nobody has measured false-accept/false-reject for a two-run oracle on agent-written patches
nodes.body: Every published weakness measurement found is conditioned on gold or top-leaderboard patches evaluated on a clean, curated base: SWE-Bench+ screened one agent's successful patches (arXiv:2410.06992), UTBoost re-scored existing leaderboard submissions (arXiv:2506.09289), PatchDiff compared three solvers against ground-truth patches on Verified (arXiv:2503.15223), and the 34/300 flaky figure is SWE-bench Lite's images, not a self-hosted runner (arXiv:2407.21787). None of these reports the two numbers the proposal needs: the rate at which a base+patched double-run accepts a wrong patch (false accept), and the rate at which it rejects a correct-but-different patch (false reject), on patches produced by an unattended loop. The nearest available proxies bracket the answer widely - 7.8% of solved patches fail the developer suite in PatchDiff, 31.08% of passes are weak-test passes in SWE-Bench+, 61.1% of suites were flagged as over-specific in Verified - and they measure different populations, so they cannot be combined into a rate. A loop operator should measure both on their own 94 tasks before trusting either.

nodes.title: A 0/1 verifier at 94 tasks resolves effects no finer than about 10 points
nodes.body: At the ledger's 94 tasks (exp-ver-001) a 0/1 verifier result gives a 95% binomial half-width of +/-10.1 points at p=0.5 (1.96*sqrt(0.25/94)=0.101); at the 458-attempt level the same arithmetic gives +/-4.6 points. Because exp-score-001 makes each attempt worth exactly one bit and exp-gate-001 shows minGain never changed a decision, every promotion in this ledger was decided at a resolution coarser than the effects claimed for it (6684 changed lines over 114 patches, exp-human-007). Mechanism: a binary gate can only report 'the same or better', so a true +2-point change and a true -2-point change are the same observation unless the sample is large. Falsifiable prediction: score the next 100 rounds the same way and the round-to-round promotion-rate change will stay inside +/-10 points at 95% confidence, so any claimed gain below that is unidentifiable from the measurement rather than absent from the system.

nodes.title: McNemar minimum detectable effect depends only on discordant pairs: 1145 pairs were needed where 500 were run
nodes.body: Paired binary data is analysed with McNemar, and the minimum detectable effect depends only on the discordant pairs: n = (z(1-a/2)+z(1-b))^2 * (p01+p10) / (p01-p10)^2. Worked instance from a public SWE-bench Verified run (single call 388/500 = 77.6%, team-solve 400/500 = 80.0%): both solved 373, team-only 27, single-only 15, neither 85, so p01+p10 = 42/500 = 0.084 and the observed difference is 0.024. Plugging in gives n = 7.849*0.084/0.000576 = 1145 pairs for 80% power at alpha=0.05, so the experiment needed roughly 2.3x the 500 instances it had; exact McNemar duly returned p = 0.09, a 2.4-point difference a naive pass-rate comparison would have called a win. The same run's own direct attempt scored 393/500 against the team's 400/500 with 7 discordant pairs one way and 0 the other, p = 0.016.

nodes.title: Pairing on the same task removes the dominant variance term and is the cheapest resolution upgrade available
nodes.body: The 94 tasks in this ledger differ by orders of magnitude in difficulty (median verifier 3 assertions, 348 total, exp-ver-001), so between-task variance swamps any policy effect; a retried task is its own control and the only quantity left is the discordance rate. The worked SWE-bench example shows why this matters: 42 of 500 pairs disagreed at all, and inference came from those 42 rather than from the 888 concordant results, which is what makes a 2.4-point difference unreadable even though the paired design is already the efficient one. It applies here because 89 of 94 verifiers pass on the clean base tree (exp-ver-003): the tasks are near-saturated, so between-task variance is small but the usable signal is smaller still. Falsifiable prediction: converting the loop from 'new task per round' to 'same task, changed policy, 20 paired retries' cuts the rounds needed to detect a 10-point effect from >100 to about 20.

nodes.title: The bottleneck is not the binary score but an oracle that is already green on 89 of 94 unpatched trees
nodes.body: 89 of 94 task verifiers pass on the clean base tree (exp-ver-003). A verifier that is already green before the patch cannot testify that the patch did anything; it can only testify that the patch did not break something, and even that only for the 3 median assertions it contains (exp-ver-001, 348 assertions across all 94 tasks). That is the real measurement bottleneck: the oracle attached to the score is too weak to separate 'fixed' from 'untouched', and the published analogue is the SWE-bench Pro audit in which five senior engineers judged 249 of 731 public tasks (34.1%) broken, with 'test scope too narrow' - a partial fix passes - counted as one of four failure classes. Falsifiable prediction: for every task whose verifier passes on base, a seeded regression in the patched lines has a >50% chance of also passing the verifier, measurable with 10 mutants per task.
nodes.source: exp-ver-003; exp-ver-001; https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.16941 (SWE-bench Pro audit, via secondary reports)

nodes.title: Published audit claims 129 of 133 adjacent system pairs are not separable on SWE-bench Verified (snippet only, unverified)
nodes.body: A paired-resolution audit (Zenodo record 22541066) is reported to take 134 systems x 500 SWE-bench Verified instances and find 129 of 133 adjacent-rank pairs not separable at the 5% level, with roughly 14,000 instances needed to resolve a 1-percentage-point gap. If true this is the cleanest published statement of the resolution limit of a 500-item code benchmark, and it is the same arithmetic as the McNemar result above. The PDF could not be fetched: both attempts returned HTTP 404 through the fetch endpoint, so this node rests on a search snippet alone and is marked low confidence. It is included because the number is load-bearing for the 'no budget for a benchmark' argument and should be re-verified against the primary PDF before being quoted, not because it has been read.

nodes.title: Google's mutation cost curve: one mutant per line, 7 per file, several minutes each, 15% productive at first
nodes.body: Google's deployment is the only public cost curve for mutation at scale: about 2 billion lines, >500,000,000 test executions per day gating 60,000 changelists, mutation restricted to changed and covered lines, at most one mutant per line, five operators (AOR, LCR, ROR, UOI, SBR), at most 7 reported mutants per file, median 2 live mutants per changelist and 99th percentile 43. Evaluating and resolving a single mutant takes 'several minutes' of developer time, and developers initially classified 85% of reported mutants as unproductive, i.e. 15% were worth acting on; six years of feedback from >20,000 developers plus arid-node suppression moved that to 89% productive over 24,000 developers and 1,000+ projects. The supporting dataset is 14,730,562 mutants over 662,584 changes in 446,604 files. Google explicitly declined to ship a mutation score because it was not actionable; they ship individual mutants.

nodes.title: A verifier mutation score buys oracle strength, not code quality, and costs at most one test run per changed line
nodes.body: A pass rate answers 'did the verifier go green'; a mutation score answers 'would the verifier have gone red if the patch had been wrong', and only the second is evidence that a promotion means anything. Concretely: take the 6684 changed lines in the 114-patch promotion queue (exp-human-007), seed at most one mutant per line - the same one-per-line cap Google uses - and score each verifier by the fraction of those mutants it kills. The compute cost is one compile-and-test run per mutant, so the whole queue is bounded by 6684 runs, a number this loop can afford in a way Google's human review cost of 'several minutes per mutant' never could. The rationale is the Buffer.view() case: the line is covered, the test asserts nothing about the appended buffer, and only a statement-deletion mutant exposes it. Falsifiable prediction: verifiers in the bottom quartile of mutation score will account for the majority of patches later repaired or reverted.

nodes.title: Same 1/3 skill reports 33%, 70% or 4% depending on how retries are counted
nodes.body: Retrying a task changes what the number means. With per-attempt success p, reporting the best of k attempts gives pass@k = 1-(1-p)^k while reporting 'solved every time' gives pass^k = p^k; at p = 1/3 and k = 3 those are 70% and 4% from the same 33% success rate (worked example in the Caliper README). For this ledger the direction is already fixed by exp-ver-003: 89 of 94 verifiers pass on the clean base tree, so retrying a solved task cannot promote anything and a pass@k-style metric would be measuring verifier saturation rather than agent skill. The actionable statistic is the opposite one: count how often the same task, retried under the same policy, flips after having been solved. Nobody in this ledger has recorded that number, and it bounds how much of the 458 attempts is signal rather than a coin landing differently.

nodes.title: A loop that peeks after every round needs a confidence sequence or alpha spending, not a per-round p-value
nodes.body: Continuous monitoring is the specific statistical hazard here, because the loop looks after every round and promotes when it likes. Repeated looks at a fixed-alpha test inflate Type I error; the two accepted fixes are group-sequential alpha spending (Pocock, O'Brien-Fleming, implemented in R ldbounds and rpact and in SAS SEQDESIGN) and anytime-valid confidence sequences built from mixture martingales, which give a valid interval at every stopping time rather than only at a pre-declared N (Anytime-Valid Inference For Multinomial Count Data, NeurIPS 2022, builds on Howard et al.). Mechanism: the martingale construction pays a modest constant factor in interval width in exchange for validity under arbitrary stopping, so the honest error bar is wider than the naive one but never wrong. For a 0/1 promotion outcome the Bernoulli form is the one to use; a per-round p-value over 'did this round promote' is not.

nodes.title: Probability of superiority beats standardized mean difference at N=5..20 on non-normal SE data
nodes.body: Kitchenham and Madeyski's simulation study (Empirical Software Engineering 29:137, 2024) is the direct authority for small-n SE measurement: SE datasets are non-normal, parametric standardized mean difference (StdMD) is biased and low-powered at the N=5, 10, 20 per-group grid their reproducer package defaults to, and the probability of superiority (p-hat, the chance a random observation from one condition exceeds one from the other) plus Cliff's d 'consistently outperformed StdMD in terms of negligible small sample bias'. p-hat's power was always at least Cliff's d's; it beat StdMD on log-normal and Laplace data and lost on normal and gamma; its Type I error was less biased in all but one condition. Their conclusion is quotable: 'Using p-hat is a low-risk option ... Parametric methods are only preferable if you have prior knowledge of the data distribution.'

nodes.title: LiveCodeBench dates every problem and only scores a model on problems released after its cutoff
nodes.body: LiveCodeBench (arXiv:2403.07974) collects problems from LeetCode, AtCoder and CodeForces from May 2023 onward and tags each with its contest release date, then evaluates a model only on problems released after that model's training cutoff; the published set is >500 problems for May 2023-May 2024 at roughly 17 tests per problem, run across 18 base and 34 instruction-tuned models. The mechanism is contamination resistance by construction rather than by audit: a problem that did not exist cannot be in the training set. The measured effect is a 'stark drop' for DeepSeek, GPT-4-O and Codestral on post-cutoff problems, and HumanEval+ shows the same direction when tests alone are strengthened (up to 8% drop), while some models are good on HumanEval and not on LiveCodeBench - direct evidence of benchmark overfitting. Their design principle 4 also warns that when most SoTA models score near zero on most items, 'the variance in performances is low', i.e. difficulty must be balanced or the benchmark stops discriminating.

nodes.title: SWE-bench Pro resists contamination by license and by private repos, and still saturated in eight months
nodes.body: SWE-bench Pro (arXiv:2509.16941) is 1,865 problems over 41 repositories split three ways: a public set of 11 repos, a held-out set of 12 repos that are not public, and a commercial set of 18 proprietary repos from partner startups whose results are released but whose problems are not. Contamination resistance is structural - copyleft (GPL) licences create legal barriers to including the code in training corpora, and the commercial repos are simply private - rather than statistical. That is the strongest available design for 'a suite the system did not author', and it still was not enough: the July 2026 audit reported the public split rising from 23.3% to 80.3% solve rate in eight months, with 200 of 731 public tasks (27.4%) flagged broken by the pipeline and 249 (34.1%) judged broken by five senior engineers, roughly the ~30% figure OpenAI itself estimated, across four failure classes (tests too strict, prompt underspecified, test scope too narrow, misleading prompt).
nodes.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.16941; secondary reports of the July 2026 audit (tmtpost, ifeng) - primary post not fetched

nodes.title: SWE-rebench is the published answer to 'a benchmark that grows': a pipeline, not a dataset
nodes.body: SWE-rebench (arXiv:2505.20411, NeurIPS 2025) replaces the dataset with a pipeline: it continuously extracts interactive SWE tasks from diverse GitHub repositories, yielding over 21,000 Python tasks usable for RL, and uses the continuous supply of fresh tasks as a contamination-free benchmark for agentic software engineering. The evaluation claim is the important part for this ledger: comparing models on the fresh stream against SWE-bench Verified shows that some models' performance 'might be inflated due to contamination issues'. The design lesson is that the unit of measurement is the collection procedure and its date, not a frozen file - a suite authored once and reused has a shelf life measured in months, whereas a suite regenerated from a rule has a shelf life set by the rule.
